reason: The chambers need muscle to squeeze, which directly supports the pump goal.
expectation: The heart muscle will surround the chambers and enable them to contract.

effect: The chambers can squeeze, but fluid can move toward both the inlet and outlet, so they need a way to direct flow.
reaction: The two flow arrows make the need for valves clear.
reason: Heart valves should prevent backward flow during a squeeze.
expectation: The valves will direct blood forward through the chambers.

effect: The valves direct flow through squeezing and refilling; the heart still needs a way to repeat its contractions.
reaction: The paired panels clearly show how the valves control flow.
reason: The pacemaker cells' spreading electrical wave suggests they can coordinate repeated heartbeats.
expectation: The pacemaker cells will help the heart squeeze repeatedly.

effect: The heart now beats in coordinated contractions, completing the pump goal. It still needs blood and a returning vessel route.
reaction: The distinction that the heart starts its own beat while nerves adjust it is interesting.
reason: Hemoglobin fits inside the red-cell envelopes and should give the cells a way to carry oxygen.
expectation: The envelopes will become oxygen-carrying red blood cells.

effect: The red blood cells can carry oxygen and make ATP from sugar without mitochondria. They still need to be combined with plasma for the blood supply.
reaction: It is interesting that these cells make ATP despite lacking mitochondria.
reason: Plasma is the fluid component available to carry the red blood cells.
expectation: The red blood cells and plasma will form blood.

effect: The red cells and plasma formed blood, so the remaining task is to connect the pump, blood and vessels into a returning route.
reaction: The inset clarifies that blood includes other components too.
reason: Capillary networks should connect the arteries and veins into a route through tissues.
expectation: The vessels will form a connected route from arteries through capillaries to veins.

effect: The arteries, capillaries and veins now form a connected circuit with slots for the pump and transport medium.
reaction: The labeled slots make the remaining fittings clear.
reason: The beating heart belongs in the circuit's pump slot.
expectation: The heart will fit into the pump slot.

effect: The beating heart is fitted into the circuit; the transport medium slot still needs blood.
reaction: The heart’s connection to both outgoing and returning vessels makes the circuit easier to picture.
reason: Oxygen-carrying blood fits the circuit’s transport medium slot.
expectation: The blood will fill the transport medium slot and complete the returning route.

effect: Adding blood completed the circuit. The exchange inset shows oxygen and nutrients reaching tissue while red cells remain inside the capillary.
reaction: The completed route was satisfying, and the exchange inset helped connect circulation to the cells built earlier.

mostWorthwhile.text: Adding the valves was most worthwhile: the squeeze and refill panels made their role in directing flow clear.

leastWorthwhile.text: Fitting the heart and blood into the labeled slots was straightforward but less engaging than figuring out how the pump worked.

surprise.text: I was interested that red blood cells make ATP from sugar despite lacking mitochondria.

arbitrary.text: No action felt particularly arbitrary; the item pictures and goals gave each combination a clear purpose.

continue.text: I would choose to continue because the chapter connected cell-level work to circulation, and I would be curious to see how another body system joins the model.
